name: Pakistan (West and East)

areaKm2.note: world_1960 Pakistan polygon (West and East wings) = ~957,000 km2 computed on the sphere. West ~803,900 + East 147,570 km2 = ~951,500 (mid); high adds the Pakistani-administered parts of Kashmir (Azad Kashmir, Northern Areas) where the polygon omits them.

population.note: Both wings included. OWID (HYDE/UN) 1971: Pakistan (today's territory) 61.8M + Bangladesh 70.3M = 132.1M. COW NMC v7 tpop 1971 = 62.4M covers the West wing only. ~10M East Bengalis had fled to India by December 1971 (low).

urbanization.note: OWID urban share 1971: Pakistan 26.5%, Bangladesh 8.5%; population-weighted (61.8M, 70.3M) = 16.9%.

activePersonnel.note: War article infobox: Pakistan Armed Forces 350,000 (Dixit 2002 p. 165) to 365,000 (Cloughley 2016). CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9) (https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-0000399238): army 284,000, air force 17,100, navy 9,700 = 310,800 (low, before the two new divisions were raised). COW NMC v7 milper 1971 = 404,000 (high). Paramilitary (~280,000 incl. EPCAF, Rangers, Razakars ~35,000) excluded.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: CIA memo: Pakistan lacks an organized reserve. Counted here: ex-servicemen, Mujahid and paramilitary that can be called up; Cooper and Ali via the Bangladesh Liberation War article give ~280,000 paramilitary for both wings (high).

supportPersonnel.note: Everything outside the infantry P roles: air force 17,100 and navy 9,700 (CIA mid-1971), plus armour (2 armoured divisions, ~1,100 tanks), artillery (1,320 pieces), engineers, signals, logistics and staffs. Mid = active minus P roles.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: Volunteer army recruited mainly from Punjab and the NWFP; the East wing (53% of population) was in revolt and not a recruitment base, so the realistic total-war ratio of the whole population is low.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Reconstruction from the CIA order of battle (mid-1971): 13 infantry divisions and 7 independent brigades (~140 battalions), plus 2 new divisions raised in 1971 with Chinese equipment, at ~800 riflemen per battalion. East Pakistan: ~91,000 regular troops of all arms (Cloughley, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War), CIA mid-1971 ~70,000 in a corps of 3 infantry divisions.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: G3 rifles and US/Chinese small arms; CIA notes complete dependence on foreign materiel

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: long-service volunteers, but CIA notes inadequate training facilities and insufficient combined-arms training

count.note: Educated guess: Special Service Group (~2,000 commandos) plus Gilgit/Northern Scouts and light Azad Kashmir units in the mountain sector.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: light infantry kit

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: SSG US-trained commandos

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): artillery including self-propelled guns 1,320 (incl. ~500 guns and AA guns from China and 60 Soviet pieces added since 1965).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: US 105/155 mm, 25-pdr, Chinese and Soviet 130 mm

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: professional artillery, 1965 veterans

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): 1,000 medium tanks (M47/M48 Patton, Chinese T-59, T-54/55, M4 Sherman) and 94 light tanks (M24, PT-76) = 1,094. CIA notes condition and operational status unknown, so low 850.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: aging Pattons, obsolete Shermans and M24s; T-59s newer

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: CIA: insufficient combined-arms training; Basantar losses

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): 100 armoured personnel carriers (M113).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: M113 era-typical

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: small mechanised component

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): Mirage IIIE 24 + F-104 8 + MiG-19 (F-6) 122 = 154; five interceptor squadrons at Sargodha.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Mirage IIIE modern, MiG-19 and F-104 era-typical, few BVR weapons

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: well-regarded pilots, 1965 veterans; CIA notes pilot shortage

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): F-86 Sabre 160 + B-57 18 + Il-28 4 = 182. Wikipedia air war article: ~290 aircraft in the West and 16 F-86 in East Pakistan.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: F-86 Sabre a Korean War-era subsonic type; B-57 aging

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: aggressive and skilled PAF pilots

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): 45 helicopters (Mi-8, Alouette III, Bell 47).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: utility helicopters

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: small army aviation

count.note: Naval war article infobox (Pakistan Navy): 1 light cruiser (Babur), 5 destroyers, 2 frigates. CIA memo: all major combatants operational except two destroyers.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: old ex-British WWII hulls, no anti-ship missiles

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: CIA: ships rarely operate outside West Pakistan coastal waters

count.note: Naval war article: 8 minesweepers and 2 ex-Saudi Jaguar fast attack craft; plus river gunboats and patrol craft in East Pakistan (7 gunboats and 3 patrol vessels lost in the war). Reconstruction.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: small, old craft

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: coastal navy

count.note: CIA Directorate of Intelligence memorandum "India-Pakistan: Comparative Capabilities in a New Military Confrontation", 13 Sep 1971, table "Military Personnel and Equipment as of Mid-1971" (p. 9): 4 submarines (3 French Daphne class, PNS Ghazi ex-US Tench class) plus 6 Italian midget submarines (not counted). Ghazi lost off Visakhapatnam on 4 Dec 1971.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: modern Daphnes; Ghazi a WWII fleet boat

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Hangor sank INS Khukri (9 Dec 1971)

count.note: Educated guess: batteries. No SAMs in 1971; army and air force AAA (Chinese 37/57 mm, US 40 mm and 90 mm). CIA: ~500 artillery and AA guns from China since 1965. At ~6-8 guns per battery.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: guns only, no SAMs

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: IAF lost most of its eastern aircraft to ground fire

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: Yahya Khan military regime; no joint plan for the East; Niazi surrendered Dacca after 13 days; poor inter-service coordination

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: strong regimental identity in the West, but Bengali units (East Bengal Regiment, EPR) defected in March 1971

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.25-0.5. Evidence: East wing garrison isolated among a hostile population after a brutal counter-insurgency; West wing morale average

weapons.note: Anchor: between 8 (1943) and 9 (1985). Evidence: Pattons, F-86, Chinese T-59 and 130 mm guns; no SAMs or guided anti-tank missiles in quantity

armor.note: Anchor: 8 (rolled homogeneous armour). Evidence: M47/M48, T-59; Shermans still in service

ships.note: Anchor: 8 (carriers, radar, submarines). Evidence: WWII destroyers and cruiser, modern Daphne submarines, no missile craft

fortification.note: Anchor: 8. Evidence: Ichhogil (BRB) Canal defences of Lahore, bunker lines; fortress towns in East Pakistan (Jessore, Jamalpur)

logistics.note: Anchor: 8 (motor transport, rail). Evidence: CIA: 60-90 days of fuel and ammunition, dependence on foreign spares; East wing supplied only by sea/air around India

communications.note: Anchor: 8 (radio at company level). Evidence: US-pattern radios; Dacca-Rawalpindi link by radio

isr.note: Anchor: ISR 8 = radar. Evidence: radar network in West Pakistan; RB-57 reconnaissance

air.note: Anchor: air 8 = 1943, 9 = 1985. Evidence: Mirage IIIE and F-104 Mach 2, but F-86 bulk

cyber.note: No military computer networks; anchor cyber 9 = 1990 networks.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID CSV) 1971: Pakistan 1,484, Bangladesh 934 (2011 int$); population-weighted (61.8M, 70.3M) = ~1,190.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: COW NMC v7 milex 1971 = 727,215 thousand current US$. World Bank GDP 1971: Pakistan (West) US$10.67bn (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/PAK/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?date=1970:1972&format=json), Bangladesh US$8.75bn -> 3.7% of both wings (low), 6.8% of the West wing (high). Mid 5% for wartime 1971.

industrialShare.note: World Bank NV.IND.TOTL.ZS 1971: Pakistan 21.1%, Bangladesh 7.7%; GDP-weighted both wings ~15%.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of the labour force (share of food output not eaten by the farm population; no calorie self-sufficiency adjustment). World Bank WDI Database Archives (version 1999 Apr), SL.AGR.TOTL.ZS "Labor force in agriculture (% of total)" (ILO-based) Pakistan (West) 1971 = 59.0% and Bangladesh (East) 1971 = 80.7%, weighted by OWID population 61.8M and 70.3M = 70.5%. Same series at https://api.worldbank.org/v2/sources/57/country/PAK/series/SL.AGR.TOTL.ZS/time/all?format=json. Share 70.5% (range 65.0-75.0%) -> 0.295 (0.25-0.35).

annualCohort.note: Males reaching military age per year, World Bank 1971: Pakistan male pop 32,964,917 x 9.333% aged 15-19 / 5 = 615,358; Bangladesh 36,329,727 x 9.602% / 5 = 697,646; total 1,313,004 (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/PAK/indicator/SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y?date=1971&format=json). Males only; range +/-10%.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: Paved roads: West wing ~25,000 km, East wing ~4,000 km (delta country with few bridges).

railKm.note: Educated guess: Pakistan Western Railway ~8,600 km plus East Pakistan Railway ~2,850 km.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: Karachi; Chittagong and Chalna in the East.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Pakistan ~0.55M GRT of merchant shipping (National Shipping Corporation and private lines) x ~1.5 dwt/grt.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: Short-range army built for border defence; CIA: 60-90 day stocks and no organized reserve; the East wing was 1,600 km away across India.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: Plough bullocks in both wings, camels and donkeys in the West; early-1970s livestock censuses.

nuclearWarheads.note: FAS estimates via OWID list no Pakistani warheads before the 1990s; the weapons programme was launched only in January 1972 (Multan meeting).

chokepoints: Sea route Karachi-Chittagong around India (~4,800 km)
Padma and Meghna rivers in East Pakistan

homeDefense.note: 1.1 row in the West wing (familiar terrain, canal defences, local supply, population support); 1.0 in the East wing where the population was hostile and supported the Mukti Bahini.

notes: Snapshot date 3 December 1971 (PAF pre-emptive strikes, Operation Chengiz Khan). Population and territory include BOTH wings: West Pakistan and East Pakistan (today Bangladesh); hb:1960:Pakistan contains both polygons. includes is empty because Bangladesh had no state of its own until 16 December 1971. Main order-of-battle source: declassified CIA intelligence memorandum of 13 Sep 1971 (https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-0000399238), table as of mid-1971; the IISS Military Balance 1971-72 and Sisson and Rose, War and Secession, were not fetchable and are not cited line by line. Theatre split for the battle agent: East Pakistan ~91,000 regular troops of all arms (Cloughley via the Bangladesh Liberation War article; CIA mid-1971 ~70,000, one corps of 3 divisions, later 2 ad hoc divisions), 16 F-86 and no submarines bar Ghazi; the rest in the West, 8+ divisions near Kashmir. Paramilitary (~280,000 incl. East Pakistan Civil Armed Forces and ~35,000 Razakars) excluded from active. Pakistan had no domestic production of major platforms in 1971 (Heavy Industries Taxila and the Kamra aircraft factories came later), so production is empty; resupply came from China, plus France for aircraft and submarines. Infantry splits are reconstructions (grade C/D).
